paragraph.text: F9. "You also kill mosquitoes and rats at home"

self-defense and real conflict are different from raising animals to eat. A mosquito that transmits dengue or malaria, or a rat that contaminates food, poses a concrete threat; a pig in a shed threatens no one. Even in cases of conflict, animal ethics asks us to prefer non-lethal methods when possible. And if killing mosquitoes were inconsistent, that would be a problem for whoever kills mosquitoes, not a justification for raising and slaughtering billions of animals.
"You use insect repellent. If there's a cockroach, you kill it. So you can't say anything."
Vegans also kill animals, such as mosquitoes, cockroaches and rats, when they cause problems.
This shows they accept killing animals for human interests.
Eating meat also serves a human interest.
So vegans can't condemn meat eaters without being inconsistent.
P1 is true in many cases. The problem lies in P2 and P3: the interest in not catching a disease or not having one's home contaminated is very different from the interest in a flavor.
fails at P3, which equates interests of very different weights.
"You also kill mosquitoes and rats at home."
"If there's a cockroach, you kill it."
"A vegan who uses rat poison is a hypocrite."
"Accepting pest control shows vegans aren't consistent."
"You use a phone, so you're a hypocrite." (which is L4)

If a mosquito can give you a disease, keeping it away is protecting yourself. That's different from raising a little pig in a cramped place just to eat it later. In one case, we defend ourselves; in the other, we make the animal be born to die. And when we can, the best thing is to keep the critters away without killing them.

Protecting yourself from a mosquito that carries disease, or from rats that contaminate food, is self-defense against a real threat. Raising an animal to eat isn't: they threaten no one. Even in these cases of conflict, animal ethics asks us to use non-lethal methods when possible, such as screens, repellents and sealing gaps. And if someone were inconsistent about mosquitoes, that wouldn't make it acceptable to raise and slaughter billions of animals.
"Was the pig who became bacon threatening anyone?"
The argument equates very different situations:
Every ethics accepts defense against real threats, including between humans. That doesn't make it acceptable to harm those who threaten no one.
Avoiding dengue or contamination is a serious interest; the taste of meat is a lesser interest that can be met in other ways (J11).

text.bold: 3. Animal ethics asks for non-lethal methods.

paragraph.text: Prevention, screens, repellents and sealing gaps are preferable to killing. Animal advocates tend to use these methods.
If someone kills mosquitoes without need, that's their problem, not permission for everyone to cause more harm. This is the tu quoque fallacy.

Raising animals for food brings billions of animals into existence every year precisely so they can die. Pest control at home responds to a concrete threat that already exists, and even so should prefer prevention and non-lethal methods.

The argument points to a real issue: conflicts with animals exist, and killing pests also involves beings who may feel. Animal advocates shouldn't pretend this is irrelevant, and should prefer non-lethal methods whenever possible.
But self-defense against a real threat is different from raising animals to eat. The first case is a hard conflict; the second is a choice that can be avoided.
